reading.body:
Government AI activity is now a matter of public record: federal agencies disclose what they run, GAO audits those inventories, and 2,425 state AI bills are tracked to their source.

The pattern is layered oversight. GAO reviews federal AI inventories and management, state legislation is tracked bill by bill, and international indexes from Oxford Insights, OECD.AI, and Stanford HAI compare national readiness, strategies, and policy execution. This makes government AI adoption measurable and auditable, which shapes where and how public-sector systems can operate.

What this record does not show is the physical layer. The Oxford Insights index scores infrastructure as one dimension, but no scores or infrastructure findings appear here. The data covers governance, law, and policy, not the compute, buildings, or power behind the systems being governed.

summary: Federal AI use is publicly inventoried; GAO audits it, and the state legislatures writing AI law are tracked on this site.

analysis.body:
The clearest measured picture of government AI use comes from GAO's audit of federal agencies. Twenty of 23 agencies reported about 1,200 current and planned artificial intelligence use cases, while three agencies reported not having uses for AI. Most of those use cases were in the planning phase rather than in production, and in about 200 instances agencies reported they were currently using AI. NASA and the Department of Commerce reported the highest number of use cases. The reported applications include analyzing data from cameras and radar to identify border activities, analyzing photographs from drones, and targeting scientific specimens for planetary rovers.

GAO also found the underlying record unreliable. Five agencies provided comprehensive information for each reported use case, while the other 15 had instances of incomplete and inaccurate data, with some inventories missing required elements such as the AI life cycle stage, and two inventories including AI uses that agencies later determined were not AI. On compliance, ten of 23 agencies implemented all AI requirements specific to them, 12 implemented some but not all, and one was exempt. GAO reported that the Office of Management and Budget had not developed guidance for the acquisition and use of AI, the Office of Personnel Management had not established or updated an occupational category for employees doing AI work, and the Office of Science and Technology Policy had not communicated which agencies were expected to fulfill specific requirements. Commerce and the General Services Administration fully implemented selected requirements, with Commerce creating a plan to develop AI technical standards and GSA establishing an AI Center of Excellence. The President's fiscal year 2023 budget request included $1.8 billion for nondefense research and development investment in AI.

The legislative side is where the volume sits. This site's AI laws tracker counts 6,015 artificial intelligence bills across 53 jurisdictions, refreshed daily from the LegiScan legislative database and linked to each bill's official page. From the enrolled text of measures states have passed, the tracker compared 103 measures across 27 states, reviewed on September 18, 2026, and found that no two states wrote the same law. Only two states passed a broad law reaching consequential decisions across sectors, Colorado in CO SB189 and Texas in TX HB149. Every other measure names one setting, such as a companion chatbot, a political ad, an insurance prior authorization, a classroom or a state agency, which is why a national company meets a patchwork.

Where the stakes are personal, the tracker reports that legislatures keep writing the same rule, that AI may assist but may not be the only decider. Insurers cannot deny care on an algorithm alone under AL SB63 and IA HF2635. AI cannot deliver therapy or present itself as a licensed clinician under IL HB1806, TN HB1470 and CA AB489. It cannot be the sole instructor of a college course or score a teacher evaluation under IL HB1859 and IL SB2909, and New York requires meaningful human review before agencies automate benefit decisions under NY S07599. On enforcement, the tracker found that no state in this set created a new agency to enforce AI law. The attorney general enforces the larger laws, often exclusively, as in CA SB53, CO SB189, GA SB540, ID S1297, IL SB0315, NY S06953, RI H7350 and TX HB149, and several states simply declare a violation to be an unfair or deceptive trade practice under their consumer protection act, including CT HB05222, HI SB3001, ME LD1727, TN HB1470 and WA HB2225. Insurance commissioners, licensing boards and election agencies handle their own sectors, and a private right to sue is the exception, appearing mainly where one identifiable person is harmed.

The cross-national and policy layer is covered by three organizations in this material. OECD.AI, the OECD Artificial Intelligence Policy Observatory, says it helps countries shape trustworthy AI with the OECD AI Principles and gives access to 900+ national AI policies and initiatives, live data about AI and a blog about AI policy, and notes that the GPAI initiative and OECD member countries' work on AI joined forces under the GPAI brand, with organisations developing advanced AI systems able to participate by submitting a report to facilitate transparency and comparability of risk mitigation measures. Oxford Insights, which produces the Government AI Readiness Index scoring nearly every country on policy capacity, governance, infrastructure and public-sector adoption, describes its work as helping governments increase the impact of their public services by empowering teams and harnessing technology. Stanford HAI's AI Index, which carries the government and policy track including legislation counts, national strategy execution and public-sector procurement, reports a widening gap between what AI can do and how prepared institutions are to manage it, with frameworks needed to govern, evaluate and understand the technology falling behind, and notes its previous editions have been referenced by high-level policymakers in the United States, the United Kingdom and the European Union.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the material points to a few practical conclusions. GAO's finding that safeguards are needed to manage AI risks, and that there is no government-wide guidance on how agencies should acquire and use AI, means the operating rules are still being written even inside the federal government. The AI laws tracker's advice is to build to the common core, which it describes as telling people when they are dealing with AI, keeping a qualified person in any decision about health, employment, benefits or education, having a crisis protocol and knowing the age of your user if your product holds a conversation, and keeping records of what the system does, because the attorney general is the enforcer you are most likely to meet. The recurring question in each state, as the tracker puts it, is never whether you use AI but what you use it for.

https://oecd.ai/.brief: OECD.AI describes itself as a policy observatory that helps countries shape trustworthy AI in line with the OECD AI Principles, and says it offers access to more than 900 national AI policies and initiatives, live data about AI and a blog on AI policy. It invites organisations developing advanced AI systems to take part by submitting a report, saying that sharing information would help make risk mitigation measures more transparent and comparable. The observatory states that the GPAI initiative and OECD member countries' work on AI combined under the GPAI brand into one integrated partnership. Its stated purpose is to help AI actors build and use systems that respect human rights and are fair, transparent, explainable, robust, secure and safe.

https://hai.stanford.edu/ai-index.brief: The AI Index, an independent program at Stanford HAI run by an interdisciplinary steering committee, says its mission is to collect and visualise globally sourced data on artificial intelligence for policymakers, researchers, journalists, executives and the public. Its current edition reports a widening gap between what AI can do and how prepared institutions are to manage it, describing technical capabilities, investment and adoption as advancing while the frameworks for governing, evaluating and understanding the technology fall behind. The Index adds that data transparency in the field is declining, which it says makes independent measurement more critical. It states that earlier editions have been cited in major newspapers and by high-level policymakers in the United States, the United Kingdom and the European Union, and that the 2024 edition, its seventh, is its largest and most comprehensive to date. The page also describes a collaboration with Dr. Elif Kiesow Cortez, who founded and leads the AI & LegTech Lab at The Hague University of Applied Sciences, on a project using a judicial decision database to improve predictability and legal certainty for providers and users of AI technology.

https://theworldofai.org/ai-laws/.brief: The page's tracker reports 6,003 artificial intelligence bills across 53 jurisdictions, refreshed daily from the LegiScan legislative database, and says a comparison of 103 measures passed in 27 states, reviewed on September 18, 2026, found that no two states wrote the same law. It states that only Colorado's CO SB189 and Texas's TX HB149 are broad laws reaching consequential decisions across sectors, while every other measure names a single setting such as a companion chatbot, a political ad, an insurance prior authorization, a classroom or a state agency. According to the page, no state in that set created a new agency to enforce AI law: attorneys general enforce the larger laws, often exclusively, and several states declare a violation an unfair or deceptive trade practice under their consumer protection act, with a private right to sue appearing mainly where one identifiable person is harmed. It also describes recurring rules that AI may assist but not be the only decider in health, benefits, therapy, teaching and teacher evaluation, and that records should be kept because the attorney general is the enforcer most likely to be met.

https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-24-1059.brief: GAO reported that federal agencies have begun implementing AI, which is defined as computing systems that “learn” how to improve their performance, but many policy requirements remain unmet. Twenty of 23 agencies listed about 1,200 AI use cases, most still in planning and only roughly 200 in production, and inventories often omitted required data such as life-cycle stage or releasability. While Commerce and the GSA fully met selected requirements, agencies like OMB, OPM, and OSTP did not, and only ten agencies met all their AI requirements, twelve met some, and one was exempt. The report notes that AI can improve government operations but also poses risks, and the FY 2023 budget request included $1.8 billion for non-defense AI R&D.
